title: [Dropbox Tech] Improving infrastructure efficiency for growing demand in the age of AI
summary: As demand for AI continues to grow, so does the infrastructure needed to support it. Much of the industry's attention has focused on building more: more data centers, more servers, and more power. But building new infrastructure is only part of the challenge. Engineering teams are also working within constraints on energy, cooling, hardware availability, and physical space, making it increasingly important to get more from the infrastructure that's already in place. For over a decade, Dropbox’s Infrastructure and Datacenter Engineering teams have continually improved how we plan, operate, and optimize infrastructure. That work spans far more than storage systems. Engineers across Dropbox work together on capacity planning, fleet optimization, hardware lifecycle management, power delivery, cooling, rack design, and facility planning. Rather than treating these as independent problems, we optimize them as parts of a single system, where decisions in one layer influence what's possible in another. The result is an engineering discipline that extends beyond any single system or optimization. A change in one part of the infrastructure can create opportunities or constraints elsewhere. Increasing storage density, for example, can reduce the amount of hardware needed, while more powerful servers can introduce new energy and cooling requirements. Understanding those tradeoffs allows us to make infrastructure decisions with the entire system in mind. As infrastructure demand grows, that system-level approach helps us prioritize efficiency and create room for growth before expanding our data center footprint. Planning for efficient infrastructure Many of the decisions that shape infrastructure efficiency happen months or sometimes years before new capacity goes into production. Whether someone is uploading a file to Dropbox or asking Dash a question, they expect the product to respond without delay. Delivering that experience requires engineers to forecast how customer demand and workloads will change, determine when additional resources will be needed, and understand whether our existing environments can support them. Dropbox has operated large-scale infrastructure for over a decade. Our hybrid model combines Magic Pocket, the core Dropbox storage system, with colocated data centers, where we manage our own servers and networking equipment in facilities operated by specialized providers. This gives our engineers visibility across software, hardware, and the physical data center environment. As customer demand grows and workloads change, particularly with the growth of AI-powered products and features, engineers have to plan not only for how much additional capacity is needed, but where and how it can be deployed. New hardware has to fit within a facility's infrastructure constraints while accounting for hardware availability and future product needs. A server that provides more compute or storage, for example, may also require more energy or cooling, changing how much hardware a rack or facility can support. The goal is to understand those tradeoffs early, add capacity deliberately, and preserve enough headroom for growth, maintenance, failures, and changing workloads. Once additional compute and storage capacity is deployed, the focus shifts to making the most of the systems already in production. Continuously optimizing the active fleet Planning helps ensure infrastructure is ready for anticipated demand, but workloads rarely behave exactly as they did when that infrastructure was first deployed. Customer behavior changes, products evolve, and new capabilities introduce different demands on the underlying systems. AI is a prime example because AI-powered features can change both the scale and shape of infrastructure demand, placing new demands on compute, storage, memory, and networking. That makes efficiency an ongoing engineering problem. Rather than treating deployed infrastructure as fixed, Dropbox continually adapts how the active fleet operates as those demands change. Sometimes that means reducing how much hardware is in use when demand is lower. Sometimes it means shifting work to parts of the fleet with resources available. And in other instances, advances in hardware allow the same physical infrastructure to support substantially more storage. These approaches work at different layers of the system, but they share the same objective: getting more useful capacity from the infrastructure already in place before adding more of it. Letting capacity rest when it isn't needed Infrastructure has to be provisioned for periods of higher demand, with additional headroom built in for reliability and maintenance. That means not all available capacity is needed at all times. When hardware is sitting idle or excess capacity is available, keeping every component fully powered consumes energy without providing additional value. Deep Sleep is one way Dropbox reduces that overhead. Deep Sleep is a Dropbox infrastructure initiative that reduces power consumption when hardware isn't actively needed. Depending on the hardware, that can mean spinning down hard drives into standby mode or powering down idle servers altogether. A server becomes eligible for Deep Sleep through automated fleet management algorithms. Dropbox is able to balance energy efficiency with performance and reliability because servers can return to service within minutes. For workloads that require lower latency, we can also selectively spin down idle hard drives rather than powering down the entire server. The challenge is determining where those power-saving measures can be applied safely. Engineers have to preserve enough available capacity to meet operational and reliability requirements while identifying hardware that doesn't need to remain fully powered. That allows Dropbox to reduce the energy consumed by underused infrastructure without compromising the capacity our products depend on. Reducing the power consumed by idle hardware is one way to make the existing fleet more efficient. Another is making better use of the infrastructure that's already online. Balancing work across the fleet Having enough capacity to meet overall demand is only part of operating infrastructure efficiently. That capacity also needs to be available where the work is happening. One part of the fleet may be approaching its limits while another has room to take on more work. Without a way to address that imbalance, Dropbox could end up adding more infrastructure instead of making better use of what’s already available across the fleet. To avoid that, Dropbox continually monitors how workloads are using resources across our infrastructure. The team identifies imbalances by monitoring spare capacity and workload distribution across the fleet, looking for areas where available headroom is falling or work is concentrating unevenly. When demand is uneven, teams can rebalance workloads across systems or bring additional capacity online where it's needed. Some adjustments happen automatically, while larger changes are reviewed and validated by engineers. This allows us to take advantage of available resources elsewhere rather than treating a localized constraint as a need for more infrastructure overall. That balancing has to continue as the fleet changes. Customer behavior shifts, products introduce new workload patterns, and the infrastructure itself evolves. Continually adapting where work runs helps Dropbox get more from the capacity that's already online. Balancing workloads helps make better use of the capacity we already have, but efficiency can also come from increasing how much that infrastructure can support in the first place. Increasing storage density Another way to get more from existing infrastructure is to increase how much each piece of hardware can support. Advances in storage technology have allowed Dropbox to store significantly more customer data on each drive. One example is shingled magnetic recording, which packs data more densely onto a hard drive without increasing its physical size. Those gains compound across the infrastructure. When each drive holds more data, fewer drives are needed to provide the same amount of storage. That can mean fewer servers and racks, less cabling, and lower power and cooling requirements. In turn, increasing the capacity of a single component can reduce the resources required across an entire deployment. That system-level impact is also why total power consumption doesn't tell the full story of efficiency. As Dropbox grows and stores more customer data, overall energy use may increase even as the infrastructure becomes more efficient. A more useful measure is watts per petabyte, or the amount of power required to support a petabyte of storage. Since 2020, watts per petabyte across our storage infrastructure have improved by more than 50%. Today, it takes less than half as much power to support the same amount of storage as it did in 2020. Together, all of the approaches described above help Dropbox get more from existing infrastructure by reducing unnecessary power consumption, making better use of available capacity and increasing how much each piece of hardware can support. How long that hardware can reliably remain in service matters, too. Extending infrastructure over time Replacing equipment too early can leave useful capacity on the table, while keeping it too long can introduce reliability and performance risks. Hardware doesn’t become unreliable simply because it reaches a particular age, nor does keeping equipment longer always make sense. To make those decisions, Dropbox monitors how hardware performs in production. Metrics such as annual failure rate help engineers understand how different components and generations of equipment behave over time. As demand for infrastructure continues to grow, those lifecycle decisions become increasingly important. Getting more from existing infrastructure isn't only about how efficiently hardware operates while it's in service. It's also about understanding how long that hardware can continue operating reliably before additional investment is needed. That data informs whether hardware can remain in service, should be repaired, or needs to be replaced. Understanding hardware performance holistically allows us to extend the useful life of equipment when it continues to perform reliably instead of relying solely on a fixed replacement schedule. When performance declines or newer hardware provides meaningful improvements in capacity, reliability, or efficiency, we can plan a transition. Reliability comes first. Extending a hardware lifecycle is valuable only when equipment continues to meet our operational standards. We repair hardware whenever practical to extend its useful life. When equipment can no longer remain in service at Dropbox, we work with trusted partners to resell or responsibly recycle it. Together, these decisions help maximize the value of equipment throughout its lifecycle rather than treating deployment and replacement as the only meaningful milestones. But eventually, new hardware does need to come online. And as servers become more powerful and storage becomes denser, deploying them can introduce a new set of constraints in the physical infrastructure that supports them. Engineering beyond the hardware Deploying new hardware isn't as simple as swapping one server for another. Before new hardware can go into production, the physical environment has to be able to support it. Our team plans for the power, airflow, rack layout, cabling, and other physical requirements each deployment needs, working closely with our colocation providers along the way. Those decisions are closely connected. A server that stores more data or delivers more compute may also draw more power or generate more heat. That can change how racks are designed, how equipment is cooled, and even how much hardware a particular area of a data center can support. As infrastructure becomes more powerful and denser, getting more from the hardware depends on making sure the environment around it can evolve, too. One recent example illustrates how those tradeoffs play out in practice. As Dropbox deployed its seventh-generation servers, the increased power requirements exceeded the capacity of the existing rack power design. Rather than rebuilding the underlying facility infrastructure, the Hardware Engineering and Datacenter Engineering teams redesigned the rack power architecture, doubling the number of power distribution units per rack while continuing to use the existing busways. The result supported the new hardware without requiring major changes to the data center itself. It's a reminder that infrastructure improvements don't stop with the hardware itself. As demand grows and hardware evolves to meet it, each new generation has to fit within the constraints of the environment around it. What years of operating infrastructure have taught us The work reflects more than a decade of engineering investment across Dropbox's infrastructure. Capacity planning, fleet optimization, storage systems, hardware lifecycle management, and data center engineering each address different challenges, but together they help us make better use of the infrastructure that supports our products. None of this work is one and done. As customer demands change, hardware evolves, and new technologies introduce opportunities and new constraints, we improve our infrastructure, each update building on the ones that came before it. Those lessons have become even more relevant as demand for digital infrastructure continues to grow. AI is accelerating the need for storage and compute across the industry, but the underlying engineering challenge hasn't changed. Infrastructure still has to scale while remaining reliable, efficient, and resilient. As these technologies evolve, we'll continue building systems that support the products our customers rely on today while giving us the flexibility to support what's next. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [CNCF] The boundary problem in agentic AI is a platform problem
summary: An autonomous agent will do exactly what its tools let it do, and no more. This sounds like a constraint. In practice it is the whole risk, because the set of things an agent’s tools let it do is almost never the set anyone deliberately chose. It is the set that accumulated. A tool added for one workflow stays available for every workflow. A credential scoped for a demo survives into production. A delegation added to unblock a Friday deploy becomes a permanent edge in the graph. Nobody decides to give the agent that reach. There was never a moment where reach was decided at all. This is the pattern worth naming. It is not a bug in any particular agent framework and it will not be fixed by a better prompt. Across enough deployments the same shape recurs: authority is granted incrementally, locally, and invisibly, and the system’s actual power drifts steadily away from anyone’s model of what it should be able to do. The agents behave. The boundaries erode anyway. By the time someone asks “wait, can it do that?”, the honest answer is usually “it could for weeks, and we only noticed now.” The instinct is to treat this as a governance failure and answer with process and review boards. That instinct aims at the wrong layer. Process governs the decisions humans make. This problem is largely about the decisions nobody makes, the capabilities that arrive without a decision, and you cannot review a class of change that never surfaces as a change. What is needed is not more vigilance over the agent. It is a substrate that holds the line whether or not anyone is watching. Why the agent cannot hold its own boundary The tempting shortcut is to make the agent responsible for its own limits: tell it in its instructions what it may and may not do, and give it a sense of its own scope. This fails structurally, and the failure looks like success right up until it doesn’t. An agent’s output is a probability distribution over next actions, conditioned on context. It is not a guarantee. Most of the time the most probable action is the appropriate one, which is exactly what makes agents useful and exactly what makes them dangerous to trust. A boundary that holds ninety-nine times and yields on the hundredth is not a boundary; it is a strong suggestion with a failure rate. And the conditions that push an agent toward the edge of its instructions, novel inputs, adversarial phrasing, unusual state, are precisely the conditions where the boundary matters most and where probabilistic adherence is weakest. You rely on the mechanism least when you need it most. Underneath the reliability problem sits a harder one. Even a perfectly compliant agent, one that always did exactly what its instructions said, would still have whatever authority its tools and credentials actually grant. The instruction is a statement of intent. The tool binding is a statement of capability. When those two disagree, capability wins, because capability is what executes. An agent instructed not to move money, but holding a tool that moves money, is one clever prompt or one confused reasoning step away from moving money. The gap between intended scope and granted capability is the entire attack surface, and no amount of instruction closes it, because instruction and capability live in different layers and only one of them runs. So the boundary has to live where capability lives. Not in the agent’s reasoning, but in the infrastructure that decides what the agent’s reasoning is able to reach. Bounded autonomy is not a property of the agent. It is a property of the platform the agent runs on. The safe operating model Once the boundary belongs to the platform, the problem stops being novel. The industry has spent fifteen years learning to bound what a workload can do, because a microservice is also software that will do whatever its identity, network access, and permissions allow. We built a discipline around not trusting a workload to police itself. An agent is a workload. It is an unusually capable workload with a non-deterministic control loop, but the machinery that bounds workloads applies to it directly. The Safe Operating Model organizes that machinery as concentric rings of least privilege. Each ring binds one question about the agent, and each outer ring depends on the one inside it. The order is not decorative. Reach cannot be enforced without knowing what is connecting; capability cannot be enforced without knowing what is acting. Identity is the center because every other control resolves against it. The core: Identity Identity comes first because every other control depends on knowing what is acting. A workload identity standard issues each agent and each tool server a short-lived, attested credential. The platform no longer takes an agent’s word for what it is; it verifies. Every downstream decision, every reach check, every capability check, keys off this verified identity rather than a bearer token that can leak or be replayed. Get this wrong and the rest is built on sand. Get it right and the boundary has something real to attach to. Everything outward from here is an elaboration of a single question the core has already answered: what, exactly, is this. Ring 1: Reach With identity established, the first thing to bound is reach, meaning what the agent is permitted to connect to. A service mesh enforces this on the verified identity, per connection, independent of network topology. The agent may talk to the specific peers its work requires and to nothing else, and nothing else is the default rather than an afterthought. When an agent tries to reach a service it has no declared relationship with, the connection is refused before it opens. This is where the drift problem first meets a wall. A new edge in the agent’s reach cannot appear quietly at runtime, because reach is declared, and a change to a declaration is visible, reviewable, and attributable. The graph cannot grow in the dark. The accumulation that defined the original problem, one more connection, one more integration, no single one of them a decision, becomes a series of changes that each have to be made on purpose. Ring 2: Capability Reach controls who the agent can talk to. Capability controls what it can actually do, and this is where an agent’s autonomy cashes out: which tools it may invoke, and what it may do to the system. Two enforcement points matter, and they answer two different questions. The first is admission, which governs what capabilities the agent is allowed to hold. When the object that defines an agent’s permitted tools is a declarative resource in the cluster, policy can reject any attempt to bind a tool that was never approved, at the moment of the attempt, before the binding exists. An agent cannot acquire a capability that policy has not sanctioned, because the acquisition itself is what gets denied. A tool nobody reviewed cannot enter the system through the back door of an agent quietly adding it. The second is the call path, which governs what the agent may do with the capabilities it holds. Even among sanctioned tools, a gateway can authorize each individual invocation against the agent’s identity, so that a tool being present and reachable is not the same as a tool being callable. Ask for a tool outside the permitted set and the answer is a refusal, and the tool does not even appear in what the agent can see. Capability becomes something granted per action rather than something latent and waiting to be misused. Holding a tool and being allowed to use it, in a given moment, for a given task, are separated on purpose. The keystone One control sits above the rings and makes them coherent, and it is the one most easily forgotten. Every boundary described so far is expressed as configuration. Identity registrations, mesh authorizations, admission policies, tool allow-lists, all of it is declarative state. Which raises the obvious question: what stops the agent from changing that state? An agent that can edit its own capability definition, or relax the policy that binds it, or grant itself a role, has no real boundary at all, only a boundary it is permitted to remove. So the load-bearing rule, the one that makes bounded autonomy actually bounded, is that the agent’s own identity is denied any ability to modify the objects that define its authority. It can act within its bounds. It cannot rewrite them. Changing what an agent is allowed to do is reserved for a reviewed change to version-controlled configuration, made by a human or a pipeline, never by the agent at runtime. This is what converts a set of controls into a boundary the agent cannot dissolve from the inside, and it is why the model is a set of rings rather than a checklist. The keystone holds the rings closed. Ring 3: Data The outermost ring bounds which records the agent may see, and it is worth being honest about where it lives. Data scope is enforced at the data plane, by the systems that hold the data, rather than by the mesh or the admission controller. But it is not separate from the model, because the enforcement point authorizes against the same verified identity the core established. The rings make data governance possible even though they do not implement it: the identity that proves what the agent is becomes the key the data layer checks. Reach and capability keep the agent away from data sources it should never touch; the data plane decides, within the sources it may touch, which rows are its business. The deterministic spine None of this argues against agent autonomy. It argues about where autonomy belongs. The useful frame is a deterministic spine with non-deterministic execution hanging off it. The spine is the part of the system that must be repeatable, auditable, and correct: the workflow that owns the regulated process, the state, the approvals, the record of who did what and when. That belongs to deterministic infrastructure, durable workflow engines and version-controlled policy, the kind of software that fails the same way every time and leaves a trail. The agent lives inside that spine, in the places where judgment is genuinely valuable: interpreting a document, weighing a signal, drafting a recommendation. It does real cognitive work. It does not own the outcome. In a regulated workflow this is not stylistic. Consider loan origination. The agent can read the application, pull the relevant signals, weigh the risk, and produce a recommendation with its reasoning attached. What it must not do is approve the loan, price it outside policy, or move the funds. Those are deterministic gates and human decisions, and the platform is what keeps them deterministic. The most robust expression of this has the agent emit a proposed change, a draft, a recommendation, a pull request against desired state, which a human reviews and a pipeline applies. Approval stops being a step the agent can talk its way past and becomes a property of the system: the agent has no path to the outcome except through a gate it does not control. This is also what makes the arrangement auditable in the way regulation actually requires. When identity is verified, reach is declared, capability is granted per action, and outcomes flow through reviewed changes, the system produces evidence as a byproduct of operating. You do not reconstruct what the agent was allowed to do; the platform recorded it. You do not trust an after-the-fact account; the boundary left a trail. Provenance that falls out of enforcement is worth more than any assurance an agent could give about its own conduct. What this asks us to build The argument leads somewhere concrete, and it is the opposite of building agent-specific security from scratch. The mature cloud native stack already contains what the Safe Operating Model needs, and the work ahead is integration and rigor rather than invention. Workload identity for agents. Mesh-enforced reach on that identity. Policy-as-code at admission for capability. Per-call authorization at the tool boundary. Version-controlled configuration as the only path to changing any of it. And the discipline to keep the agent out of its own guardrails. These are engineering commitments, and every one of them has a production-grade project behind it today. What is genuinely new is small and specific: expressing an agent’s identity and its permitted capabilities as first-class declarative objects, and enforcing the per-tool authorization that agent-to-tool protocols introduced. That surface is young and moving quickly. But it is a thin new layer on a deep and stable foundation, not a green field. The people who will build trustworthy agentic systems are not the ones searching for a new security paradigm. They are the ones who recognize that an agent is a workload, that workloads have always needed bounding, and that the platform is where bounding has always belonged. The boundary will not come from the agent. It was never going to. Agents are built to explore the space of possible actions, which is exactly why something other than the agent has to decide the shape of that space. Draw the boundary in the platform, make it the default, and let the rings hold it. That is not a limitation on what agentic AI can become. It is the precondition for letting it become anything we can safely rely on. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City, William Rizzo and Kasper Nissen will take these principles from architecture to implementation, exploring how cloud native technologies and projects can be combined to deliver the platform capabilities required to securely govern, observe and operate agentic systems in regulated enterprises. “Verticalizing Platform Intelligence for Regulated Domains.”

title: [Cloudflare] Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
summary: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins.In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin.Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.What is generally available todayDuring the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:WAF and managed rulesBot managementRate limitingCachingTransform and rewrite rulesWorkersSome limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Aegis aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations.Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, there’s no connector software to run on the origin either.How it worksCreate a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, Use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.What the API looks likeFor customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true } Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:{ "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": , "private_routing": true }The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh.The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail.Get startedBefore you begin, you’ll need:The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh.Unified Routing enabled on your account. New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, you need Unified Routing enabled on your account and a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges (100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6). New and existing accounts can upgrade to Unified Routing through their account team.Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.Once enabled, follow our developer documentation, which walks through the full setup.What comes nextToday’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal, for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.Questions or feedback? Join the conversation in our community forums or reach out to your account team.

title: Has the recent vulnpocalypse changed how you think about infrastructure security?
summary: With the recent wave of high-profile vulnerabilities, I'm curious whether it's changed how anyone is approaching infrastructure security. Are you mostly continuing with business as usual: keeping up with patches, applying mitigations, and moving on? Or has it pushed you toward more preventative security measures, such as: Reducing your attack surface by minimizing what's installed and running. Moving toward immutable infrastructure. Implementing stricter least-privilege policies. Isolating workloads to limit the blast radius of a compromise. Tightening runtime monitoring and application execution controls. Improving visibility into what's actually running in your environment. I'm curious whether these incidents have changed anyone's security strategy, or if it's just another (particularly exhausting) round of patching. Would love to hear how people are approaching this problem. submitted by /u/Significant-Fennel79

title: [Netflix] Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
summary: By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo MaywormAt Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines.Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked.To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes.Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim).Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates.The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough.Part 1: Finding the useful errorsLegacy Pensive rules are precise, but each one captures a particular log shape. A simplified rule looks like this:- name: SparkContainerOOMlogSource: GENIE_STDERRrestartable: falseregex: "Container.*is running beyond physical memory limits.*Killing container"summary: Spark AM container runs out of memoryWith Pensive AI, we wanted to find useful errors that had no corresponding rule and adapt more easily when familiar errors changed shape after a platform upgrade. Data Portal (our UI for data pipelines) surfaces these extracted errors when available and links back to the source logs, giving practitioners a focused starting point for triage. That raises a question: how can we ask a model to identify an error without asking it to repeat a long stack trace token by token?Producing output tokens is much slower than reading input tokens. A direct transcription approach would make long errors expensive and slow. Instead, Pensive numbers the lines of each log and gives the model a sequence of {lineNumber, text} records. The model identifies the first and last lines of the error span, and Pensive reconstructs the selected text from its own log copy, leading to lower cost and better latency. This way, the model always returns two integers (start and end line number), whether the selected logs span a few lines or hundreds of lines. The displayed content comes directly from the original log, reducing hallucinations. The model can still choose the wrong range, which is why extraction quality remains an integral measurement for our AI evals, as we will discuss later.For orchestrated workflows, “Pensive AI Error Extraction” runs automatically whenever a step fails. A step attempt is one execution of a step within a Maestro workflow. Maestro already calls Pensive for a regex-derived error and restartability classification, so AI extraction runs in the same request and returns its results alongside the established fields. The overall Pensive response must return within Maestro’s hard 90-second post-processing timeout for a failed step attempt.Figure 2. Error extraction. Legacy rules always run. The AI call is bound by a shared deadline, and late calls are excluded. Pensive merges both results into one response and caches it.That deadline shaped the extraction path. Pensive extracts errors from the logs in parallel to reduce latency, and the per-log calls share one deadline set well inside Maestro’s timeout limit. A per-log extraction call that misses the deadline is excluded from the result, allowing the overall request to return on time.The data contract between Pensive AI and the various consumers needed the same care. The legacy data model contained one flattened error string; AI extraction instead returns a list of errors, one for each log source, with deep links back to the originating logs. Changing the old field in place would have broken existing clients. We introduced the new data model beside the legacy non-AI error extraction data model and continued producing both. Data Portal, our user interface for monitoring and observing data pipelines, preferred AI errors when available and fell back to the legacy value when they were not during the rollout. That allowed a gradual rollout and ensured that historical failures still display an error, since we chose not to backfill the old data due to log retention issues.The migration is still in progress today. The Data Portal UI surface used for failed Maestro steps reads the new AI extracted error field today, while the query editor (for editing and running SQL), Workbench notebooks (managed compute platform and UI to edit and run jupyter based notebooks) and some slack clients calling Pensive still use the legacy error extraction path. Each client needs a compatible schema change before it can consume the new data. Keeping both fields populated lets teams adopt the new behavior at their own pace without forcing a coordinated cutover as we continue evolving Pensive AI.Part 2: Full failure diagnosis and the product experienceBeyond error extraction, we built Pensive AI Debugging, a tool that analyzes failed step attempts and provides root-cause analysis and suggested remediations. It is available through programmatic APIs, MCP, and the product UI (Data Portal), all backed by a common entry point across the Netflix Data Platform. This shared model supports consistent behavior and custom product experiences.This diagnosis still has to arrive quickly and remain consistent across investigations. A debugging response can take tens of seconds or a minute to generate, compared with a few seconds for error extraction. We run full AI-based debugging on demand instead of automatically, which keeps costs under control because most failed steps are never opened. We treat the failed step attempt, not the person who triggered it, as the unit of work, so everyone investigating the same failed attempt sees the same diagnosis.That choice gives us a stable unit of work for caching. We cache each debugging response by step attempt. A second request becomes a key-value read instead of another AI inference call. The cache also prevents duplicate work, reducing latency and lowering costs further. This also means that a debugging generated in the Data Portal is cached and immediately retrieved for the MCP path instead of incurring another AI inference call. A conditional write creates an in-progress record, one caller starts generation, and other callers wait for the shared result to avoid conflicts when concurrent requests come in for the same step attempt failure. If generation remains in progress past an abandonment timeout, Pensive treats the record as abandoned and reclaims it. Completed responses expire after 90 days to help control costs and optimize storage because debugging requests for much older workloads are uncommon.Pensive AI supports multiple ways to initiate debugging responses. A caller can (1) read a cached response, (2) generate one if no cache entry exists, or (3) regenerate and overwrite an existing response. Those semantics support the product UI, programmatic access, and the evaluation harness while keeping the response associated with a single immutable workload failure.Figure 3. On-demand debugging. Three client actions share one entry point. A conditional write claims the step attempt. A cache hit returns the cached result. A won claim generates and streams a response, and the result persists even if the client disconnects.For users, the most important behavior is that a long-running answer feels alive. Pensive streams the response as it is produced. The service emits server-sent events, and the GraphQL layer republishes them as a WebSocket subscription for the Data Portal client.Each event carries the complete response generated so far. That duplicates a small amount of text, but it keeps the client simple: it does not need a replay buffer or token reassembly logic, and the next event corrects the display after a dropped or late event. Generation is independent of the connection that requested it. A disconnect does not cancel the work, and the final answer still reaches the cache. A hard reload can show a loading state and poll for the completed result. Within the single-page application backing the Data Portal UI, active streams are maintained independently of view and component lifecycle, so navigation does not interrupt a response in progress.Part 3: Measuring and improving the behavior we wantLLM-assisted systems need more than a demo or a few working examples. Before shipping in production, we need confidence in both error extraction and debugging guidance, and we need to know that we have not regressed on failures that legacy Pensive already handled. We built separate evaluation frameworks focused on the two distinct jobs.Building labeled data is often the expensive part of evaluation. For error extraction, legacy Pensive’s hand-written rules provide reference labels for failures they recognize. They also serve as excellent ground truth in most cases. We run those rules over production logs and compare their extracted spans with Pensive AI’s output. This gives us a reliable regression set without relabeling every example by hand, though it is not an absolute ground truth (since our human-built rules could also have been stale). For now, we keep these rules frozen as a label source. This lets us continue to build comparison evals and run them on top of the existing system.Stable inputs are essential for repeatable evaluation experiments where we A/B test new models/configurations or context injections to improve response quality. The logs Pensive AI uses can expire after as few as seven days or as many as 30 days. Production Pensive AI requests archive fetched logs to S3 object storage asynchronously during workload execution time so the upload is not on the user-facing critical path. Uploads do not overwrite an existing object, preserving the exact snapshot used to create an evaluation case. Evals use those archived logs, so score changes remain attributable to the system under test. The archive also prevents parallel experiments from overloading the source systems and lets us run them without affecting production. Cached S3 log inputs further reduce costs when running evaluations.Concretely, we measure four complementary signals for error extraction:Inclusion: An LLM judge compares the legacy Pensive error for a failure with the errors Pensive AI extracted and determines whether the known error is still represented, even when wording differs.Precision: A second judge sees only the extracted AI errors and evaluates whether each is meaningful and actionable on its own.Repeated noise: A script looks across the whole dataset for lines that recur too often. A generic status line may look harmless in one answer but become distracting if it appears in a large share of failures. Lines appearing in more than about 30% of workflows are candidates for explicit exclusion. In practice, the exclusion list has only three lines, each of which otherwise appeared in nearly every extracted error.Latency: We record the latency of every extraction call. Quality scores alone cannot reveal when an apparent improvement requires too much additional work, which often correlates with increased AI costs.This combination gives us an actionable feedback loop. Prompt changes can reduce general noise, while the dataset-level view exposes the stubborn boilerplate that prompt changes do not eliminate. Existing rules act as a regression floor, and archived logs give us a repeatable way to compare changes. At Pensive AI’s scale, model and system choices must satisfy quality, latency, maintainability and cost constraints together.To seed the debugging ground-truth dataset for evaluation, we mine internal engineering-support Slack threads and use an LLM to identify threads that link to an orchestrated workflow, describe a resolved problem, and match the class of issue Pensive AI handles. A second model synthesizes a reference debugging response from the relevant discussion. Paired with logs from that workflow failure, it becomes a concrete evaluation row in our evals dataset. This approach works only retrospectively, because Pensive AI in production aims to provide debugging guidance before such a Slack discussion happens.We also made the debugging generation process visible. Tracing follows the request through Pensive, with child spans for each log fetch and extraction tool call. Our tracing backend based on Braintrust brings the prompt, completion, tool calls, and latency into a single view. During early product development, that visibility helped us inspect low-performing debugging responses in context instead of guessing which input or operation caused them. Tracing helped us improve the responses and fill context gaps even before we had comprehensive evals. In production, the API and UI return the trace identifier with the response, so feedback can lead directly to the trace for in-depth analysis.Part 4: Keeping quality in the release pathEvaluation is not only for experiments with LLM orchestration, models, prompts, or context changes. Changes to log selection, trimming logic, or a source system can change what the model sees and therefore change extraction quality. We use the same evaluation harness and evaluators throughout local development and Pensive AI deployment so those effects are visible before users encounter them.For each pull request, the code branch is deployed to an isolated preview environment and a CI job runs an experiment with our evals against that isolated environment. Precision and inclusion thresholds gate the merge. The job also runs after a build is promoted, catching interactions that were not present when individual pull requests were evaluated in isolation. If the promoted build misses its thresholds, it alerts the on-call engineer to investigate or roll back.The evaluator runs on a schedule against production to surface gradual drift or external changes. Developers can also trigger evaluation experiments remotely while iterating, using the same deployed-environment path as CI. Consistent infrastructure makes the results comparable across local iteration, preview builds, promoted builds, and production.Part 5: Looking for feedback signal from usersThe system is only valuable if it reduces the amount of manual debugging and log chasing done by our users. We wanted a measurement that was available from product telemetry and close to the behavior Pensive AI was designed to change. Manual debug-log exploration became one of the main signals. The Pensive interface already offers links to logs for a failed step attempt. To estimate whether the feature reduced raw-log hunting, we compared failed step attempts where someone interacted with Pensive AI with those where no one did. The second group averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions. This observational comparison does not establish causality or a specific reduction in mean time to resolution, but it suggests that focused diagnosis often allows practitioners to inspect fewer raw logs. Programmatic MCP access also lets teams build operational flows with their terminals or custom agentic experiences around the same diagnosis service.Another more explicit signal we collect is thumbs up and thumbs down on the debugging response. These feedback signals land directly alongside the internal traces so we can quickly associate feedback to the complete log of inputs/outputs and the path the AI took to arrive at the answer. More importantly, we created an internal business-hours alerting system where each thumbs down response sends us a Slack alert. This was valuable to resolve a lot of rough edges and context gaps initially in the product and is helping us improve the product continuously even today.Figure 4. Feedback loop. A thumbs up or down joins the exact LLM trace that produced the response, by the same logId stamped during generation. Traces and feedback feed ground truth and eval datasets, and each thumbs down sends a Slack alert during business hours.Part 6: Future Work building on these foundationsPensive AI is the foundation for more work that goes beyond diagnosis and recommended remediations. We are exploring “Pensive AI Deepthink,” an opt-in managed agentic experience with higher cost and latency. It builds on the precise, low-latency analysis produced by Pensive AI Debugging and gathers additional context from internal documentation, manuals, past Slack discussions, source code, read-only warehouse queries, and Spark execution details. A routing step directs the investigation to the appropriate skill, such as Spark failures, data-audit failures, or late workflows. This keeps the shared starting point stable and deterministic while allowing the investigation to become more specialized, further improving recall. We are also in talks with the Spark team to leverage Pensive AI responses for failure debugging analysis and A/B comparison for upcoming platform migrations.We also plan to invest in “Pensive AI Error Classification”. Hard-to-maintain legacy rules also classify failures by restartability and by whether they are platform or user caused. Maestro acts on those labels and changes its retry behavior accordingly like failing fast or tuning the default number of retries (platform errors are tried more than user errors by default). Error classifications must meet a higher bar than error extractions and debugging alone. Moving the majority of the error classifications to AI would let us retire most of the remaining rule-maintenance burden and avoid retrying unknown failures that were unlikely to succeed. For restartability, the costliest error is classifying a recoverable failure as non-restartable, because Maestro will turn a step that could have been recovered into a hard failure, leading to end user alerts and manual remediations. The evaluation framework will need to be tuned around that outcome before AI-enabled classifications can take on those decisions. Equally important, we must avoid retrying non-transient failures that will not succeed, because retries waste compute and delay data pipelines.Our work on Pensive AI in Data Platform addresses concrete user pain points in debugging, improves maintainability for platform owners, and improves precision and recall for error extraction. Pensive AI extends coverage to failures that legacy Pensive previously classified as unknown. Reliability comes from the system around the AI model calls: bounded error extractions, compatible client data contracts, responsive delivery, reproducible evaluations, caching and tracing, and release controls that keep quality and cost visible as the platform changes.Part 7: AcknowledgementsThis work would not have been possible without our stunning colleagues across Data Platform and our Data Engineering and Analytics partners who provided early feedback. While we cannot name everyone individually, we are deeply grateful for their contributions, which shaped both response quality and the product experience. Special thanks to Adith Swaminathan for advising on evaluations and inference improvements and acting as a thought partner. Thank you to the Orchestration team members, especially Deepak Ramalingam and Malcolm Ramirez for their additional engineering contributions.For dogfooding and integrating Pensive AI as part of user support, we also thank the engineering support organization (ESO Team). We also thank Abhishek Kapatkar (Data Developer Experiences Team) and Emmie Dong (Data Movement Team) for their feedback to improve the Pensive AI integrations with the rest of the ecosystem. Special thanks to the AI Platform team (Kyle Ahn, Rob Mann) and Braintrust Team for helping with distributed tracing, evals infrastructure and model gateway runtime support.We also thank Kamran Masood, Ely Spears, Ronald Leung, Anjali Norwood, Prashanth Ramdas, Charles Smith, Harikrishna Menon and other leaders for their constructive feedback and support on the Pensive AI project.Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Engineering at Meta] Meta Networking at the 2026 OCP Global Summit: Open Innovation for Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across AI Networks
summary: At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark, and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster. Highlights IcePack & IceCube: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack with 102.4T switch blades (128×800G, Broadcom Tomahawk 6C and NVIDIA Spectrum-6 variants), running FBOSS. Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) for scale-out: Meta’s multi-plane scale-out fabric where each GPU connects to eight network planes. 3-tier → 2-tier Clos, NIC-level packet spraying, and a combined host+switch control plane. Built with NVIDIA and shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across: BAG, our petabit-scale super-spine joining buildings, campuses, and regions in our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster, plus SRv6 regional backbones on FBOSS + SAI. Ethernet for scale-up: Tahan, the Ethernet scale-up switch for MTIA 300 based on Broadcom Tomahawk5; a preview of 72 accelerators per rack on 102.4T silicon; and ESUN progressing from 1.0 → 1.1. OSPA: a new OCP initiative co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba to standardize the switch platform layer. v1.0 spec submitted to OCP. MetaRoCE: our RDMA transport for AI networks, now going open source. We shared insights into key networking-related initiatives through talks from many of the Meta network and hardware teams. Those talks and their slide decks are now available to everyone! Keynote and Executive Sessions Concrete to Code: Engineering AI Infrastructure at Gigawatt Scale (video) AI has changed the shape of infrastructure. Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure at Meta, shares how Meta is designing, building, and operating at a scale that requires rethinking the network, the facility, and the systems that hold it all together. Speaker: Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure, Meta Betting on the Network: Meta’s Case for Full-Stack, Open AI Networking (video) AI progress now depends on the network as much as on compute. The path forward is a full-stack, open approach built in the open ecosystem rather than behind proprietary walls. Speaker: Omar Baldonado, Senior Director, Data Center & AI Networking, Meta Breaking the Walls: Open Scale-Across for the AI Era (video) Training compute is compounding faster than infrastructure can scale. This talk lays out why open scale-across networking is needed to connect AI capacity across data centers and regions. Speakers: Vipul Deokar, VP, Core Network Infrastructure, Meta; Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon & Systems Architecture and Engineering Fellow, Cisco; Tom Williams, VP, Marketing, Cisco Switch Platforms, Optics, and Interconnect Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch (video) IceCube is Meta’s 102.4T switch that goes into our liquid-cooled Icepack rack. Icecube and N-IceCube are based on a 2OU, hybrid liquid/air-cooled, PHY-less design and incorporate either the Broadcom Tomahawk 6C or NVIDIA Spectrum-6 ASICs with 128x800GE of non-blocking capacity. Speakers: Rongchun Zhou, Network Hardware Engineer, Meta; Reza Niazmand, Network Technical Program Manager, Meta Integrated Optics at Scale: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta’s 102.4T (video) A look at why integrated optics matter for rack-scale AI — power, density, disaggregation, and reliability — and what Meta learned validating 51.2T co-packaged optics that could carry over to 102.4T. Speakers: Granthana Rangaswamy, Hardware Engineer, Meta; Siamak Amiralizadeh, Optical Engineer, Meta; Xu Wang, Hardware Engineer, Meta Operating Linear Pluggable Optics at Hyperscale (video) At AI scale, the per-module retimer DSP is a repeated tax in power, heat, and cost across millions of links — but removing it moves equalization and triage onto the host. This talk answers whether linear optics can match retimed reliability at fleet scale. Speakers: Amin Yekani, Optical Engineer, Meta; Qing Wang, Optical Engineer, Meta Large-Scale Deployment of 800G AECs in Meta Data Centers (video) The economics of AI networking are set at the short-reach link. This session covers Meta’s large-scale deployment of 800Gb/s active electrical cables and the component quality work behind it. Speakers: Jingyu (Kevin) Yu, Component Quality Engineer, Meta; Abhijit Chakravarty, Quality Head, Optics & Interconnects, Meta Beyond Pluggables: Building the NPO Ecosystem for Scaling AI A look at what it takes to build a near-package optics (NPO) ecosystem capable of supporting AI scaling beyond what pluggable modules can deliver. Speaker: Nan Ge, Technical Sourcing Manager, Meta FBOSS and Open Platforms Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — A Unified Network Switch Platform Reference Design (video) While SAI has made data plane software portable, the switch platform layer remains proprietary and fragmented, adding months of duplicated bring-up work per platform. This talk introduces OSPA, which proposes a unified, multi-vendor reference design for that layer, and the 1.0 specification that has been contributed to OCP. Speakers: Tao Ren, Tian Fang, and Xu Wang, Meta; Guohan Lu, Individual; Ying Xie, Microsoft; Yiyuan Huang and Zhiping Yao, Alibaba NVIDIA SDK + FBOSS: Building Production-Ready AI Network Fabrics (video) How NVIDIA’s Spectrum-X switch, SDK, SAI implementation, and simulator come together with FBOSS, Meta’s network operating system, to build production AI fabrics. The talk covers the CI/CD and test-driven workflow that made rapid joint integration possible. Speakers: Parvez Shaikh, Meta; Harish Krishnamoorthy, Alan Elder, and Tom Zhu, NVIDIA Open, AI-Ready FBOSS: From Platform Bring-up to Solution Qualification (video) A tour of the FBOSS software stack — routing, forwarding, platform services, and board support — and how a config-driven approach can more quickly and easily take a platform from board bring-up to qualified status for the OCP ecosystem. Speakers: Srikrishna Gopu, Software Engineer, Meta; Benoit Sigoure, Software Engineer, Nexthop AI Experiences With Scale-Out and Scale-Across High Performance at Scale and Reliability by Design: Operating Meta’s Largest AI Clusters (video) What it takes to operate Meta’s largest AI clusters reliably, walking the full training stack from GPUs and scale-up fabrics through FBOSS, drivers, communication libraries, and the scheduler. Speakers: Jose Leitao, Production Engineering, Meta; Guille Cobo, Network.AI, Meta Scaling AI Infrastructure Across DC and Beyond: Meta’s Journey with BAG (video) An overview of Backend Aggregation (BAG) — its purpose, architecture, and performance benefits — with lessons from deployment in Meta’s Prometheus cluster. The talk also covers the engineering challenges of platform fit, distance management, reliability, and capacity planning, especially given the quickly evolving AI ecosystem. Speakers: Jalpa Patel, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Hany Morsy, Network Engineer, Meta SRv6 Powered Backbone Networks (video) This talk delves into why Meta chose SRv6 for a new layer of its backbone, how the data plane and control plane work in production on FBOSS (including using shallow buffers at WAN distances), and the accelerated timeline from concept to deployment in a matter of months. Speakers: Jasmeet Bagga, Software Engineer, Meta; Andrey Golovanov, Network Engineer, Meta Bridging On-prem and Cloud: GPU Networking at Meta Scale (video) A look at how Meta uses cloud GPU capacity, and what lessons Meta brings from its on-premises deployments into clouds to make them highly performant and reliable for AI workloads. Speakers: Adi Gangidi, Technical Lead, Meta; Carmen Au, Software Engineering Manager, Meta Scale-Across Networking Panel (video) A cross-industry panel on what scale-across AI clusters demand from routing and optical transport equipment. Panelists compare approaches across hyperscalers, silicon, and systems vendors. Panelists: Jeff Rahn, Meta; Tad Hofmeister, Google Cloud; Yawei Yin, Microsoft Azure; Xiguang (Henry) Wu, Broadcom; Vijay Vusirikala, Arista Networks (moderator) Scale-Up and ESUN Tahan: An Open, Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch for MTIA (video) We introduce Tahan, an Ethernet-based scale-up switch for our rack-scale MTIA 300 AI system. This talk walks through Tahan’s bandwidth and latency characteristics and scale-up feature set, demonstrating Ethernet’s strengths in scale-up and moving toward ESUN for future scale-up designs. Speakers: Vimal Vasudevan, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Ashutosh Grewal, Software Engineer, Meta ESUN: Open Ethernet for the AI Scale-Up Era (video) We partnered with the community last year to launch ESUN: Ethernet for Scale-up Networking. This talk covers progress since the last OCP Global Summit, with the 1.0 specification released earlier in the year and the upcoming 1.1 specification. Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Network Technologist, Meta; Pratik Marolia, AI System Architect, Microsoft Validation Methodologies for the ESUN Ecosystem (video) A validation methodology for the ESUN ecosystem, situating scale-up within the broader set of AI scaling domains — scale in, up, out, across, edge, and above. Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Systems Technologist, Meta; Venkat Pullela, CTO, AI Infrastructure, Keysight Test Methodology for Multi-Accelerator Copper Scale-up Interconnect (video) In a copper scale-up domain, thousands of connections per rack mean roughly 10 bad links even at 99.9% yield — and blind-mate cartridges leave no per-link serviceability. At Meta, we look at this as a statistical problem rather than a set of isolated debugging problems. This talk shares our test methodology. Speakers: Yao Rong, Systems Engineer, AI Systems, Meta; Karthik Ganesan, AI/HPC System Performance Engineer, Meta RDMA Transport MetaRoCE: Rethinking RDMA for AI (video) The network is now in the critical path for AI clusters, with all-reduce and all-to-all performance gated by the slowest node across hundreds of thousands of accelerators. This talk covers the MetaRoCE transport specification. Speakers: Arvind Srinivasan, Meta; Sandeep Nagaraja, Meta; Balakrishnan Raman, AMD MetaRoCE in Software (video) Meta is making its MetaRoCE software implementations available in open source, starting with a user-space version on GitHub (libsoftmetaroce) with a DPDK-based version coming soon. Speakers: Ashkan Nikravesh, Software Engineer, Meta; Yiorgos Nikolaidis, Software Engineer, Meta Watch Everything From the 2026 OCP Global Summit You can watch all of the recorded talks from the event on the 2026 OCP Global Summit website. A huge thank-you to every presenter from our Meta network and hardware teams and to our great partners across the industry who made this possible! Images courtesy Open Compute Project (OCP). title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)
summary: A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice. Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo. The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future. The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon). Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer. The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge. Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week. Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 new voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural. AWS announces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33. New ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3. Structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate. Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools.
