title: [Netflix] Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
summary: By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform TeamQuasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decisionAt Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:Does any consumer still call this method?Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:What changed in the library’s public API?Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.From API Changes to Consumer ImpactExisting techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.Consider this simplified API change:public interface Client {- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);}For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind, r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_pathFROM requested_changes cJOIN quasar.symbol_refs r ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonicalrequested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.Bringing the Analysis Before ReleaseVersion-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:{ "change": "REMOVED", "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)", "affectedRepositories": 137, "versionDistribution": , "sampleConsumerLocations":  }, { "repository": "client-wrapper", "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java", "lines":  } ], "libraryCriticality": { "tier": 1, "basis": "highest-tier downstream application" }, "comparison": { "baseShaFound": true, "headShaFound": true }}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceedA Polyglot Foundation with SCIPThe shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.Moving Risk Assessment EarlierToday, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.What We LearnedBuilding this workflow led us to four practical lessons.Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possibleRelated TalksFrom Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Scale reservoir uncertainty analysis with agile reservoir modeling
summary: Turn subsurface uncertainty into decision-ready insight Drilling campaigns are among the most expensive and operationally complex activities in the energy industry. Rigs, crews, equipment, and logistics are scheduled months in advance, leaving little room for delay. Every hour of downtime can carry significant costs. Geoscientists and engineers rely on reservoir models to understand the subsurface and guide drilling decisions, often under intense time pressure. Yet the current modeling infrastructure that many companies rely on for these critical decisions was designed for smaller datasets, simpler workflows, and siloed operations. As subsurface data grows in scale and complexity, teams need a faster, more connected way to transform uncertainty into actionable decisions. Now generally available, agile reservoir modeling (ARM) from SLB, integrated with Azure Data Manager for Energy (ADME), is co-engineered for cloud scale to close that gap. The combined solution connects ensemble-centric reservoir modeling and simulation with a governed data foundation, elastic Azure high-performance computing, and scalable storage designed for the throughput and concurrency of large ensemble studies. Ensemble modeling evaluates hundreds of model realizations together, giving asset teams a broader view of potential outcomes and a stronger basis for understanding uncertainty and risk. ARM addresses this barrier by distributing realization generation and simulation across elastic Azure high-performance computing, while scalable storage provides the capacity, throughput, and parallel access required by ensembles of different sizes. Azure high-performance computing executes multiple realizations in parallel. As simulations complete, SLB reservoir engineering services manage the resulting ensembles and use OSDU search capabilities on ADME to support discovery, filtering, and sorting across large studies. Teams can locate relevant realizations and supported, published results without manually navigating disconnected project stores. Engineers can analyze ensembles in the reservoir engineering workspace or load them back into Petrel software for further interpretation, history matching, and reservoir engineering studies. This allows teams to work in the environment and application best suited to each task while maintaining continuity, without having to step outside their workflow to manage orchestration. ADME provides entitlement-based access control integrated with Microsoft Entra ID and supports compliance controls such as OSDU legal tags. Connecting ARM workflows to this governed data foundation helps maintain consistent access and compliance as corporate subsurface data is used across modeling and simulation. Microsoft and SLB engineering collaborated closely to build the integration between Petrel software and ARM for enterprise-scale performance. For reservoir engineers and asset teams, ARM turns ensemble modeling into a repeatable workflow rather than a bespoke infrastructure project. Teams can stress-test development concepts against calibrated ensembles that honor observed production history, not simply run a larger number of models. As new wells are drilled and new data becomes available, they can update their reservoir understanding without waiting for a major model rebuild. For energy IT and data leaders, the workflow connects simulation to an OSDU standard-aligned architecture with consistent identity, governance, search, and interoperability, reducing isolated data copies and disconnected applications. The future of the reservoir lifecycle Building on this partnership, Microsoft and SLB are working within the OSDU community to advance a more cloud-native standard for reservoir data. This work will help models, simulation results, and engineering workflows operate more consistently across applications, improving interoperability while reducing dependence on proprietary formats and silos. A shared, governed data foundation also paves the way for AI and agentic experiences that can discover data, coordinate workflows, and surface insights across the reservoir lifecycle. Combined with Azure-scale compute and storage, this creates a path toward more automated and continuous reservoir modeling. title: [GitLab] Extend GitLab Duo Agent Platform into your business systems
summary:
Developers mostly use GitLab Duo Agent Platform where they already work: the IDE, merge requests, and issues. But DevSecOps teams also support the business systems the rest of the company runs on, and those systems break too.In Salesforce, for example, when a validation fails, a callout times out, or a null slips through a trigger, the error gets logged, but the log doesn’t explain the cause. An engineer still has to read the stack trace, find the class in the repository, check what changed recently, and decide whether this is a one-off or a regression. Meanwhile, the business user who hit the error has to wait.When your Salesforce metadata lives in GitLab and ships through GitLab CI/CD, the code that explains the error is already there. In this tutorial, Salesforce calls a custom GitLab Duo Agent Platform flow through the Flows API the moment an error happens. The flow investigates the code, and your team gets a GitLab issue that already contains the root-cause analysis.Along the way, three parts of the GitLab platform work together: GitLab Duo Agent Platform investigates the error, a GitLab issue tracks the work, and GitLab CI/CD runs the flow and ships the fix.Salesforce is the example we’ll walk through in this tutorial, but the same approach works for any system that can make an HTTP request.What you'll buildSalesforce makes one call to GitLab. A custom flow in GitLab Duo Agent Platform does the rest.Errors reach GitLab Duo Agent Platform automatically from your Apex error handling, or on demand from a button. Either way, the same Apex job calls the Flows API, and the flow opens an issue with its analysis.PrerequisitesGitLab Premium or Ultimate, on GitLab.com or GitLab 19.5 and later. The Flows API used in this tutorial is generally available from 19.5.GitLab Duo Agent Platform turned on, with custom flows allowed for your top-level group.Your Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) stored in a GitLab project. This is the project the flow will read.A Maintainer or Owner role in that project.In Salesforce, permission to create a Named Credential, a custom metadata type, and Apex classes.Your Salesforce deployments must be running through a GitLab CI/CD pipeline, so the fix can ship from the same issue.Step 1: Write the triage flowStart in GitLab, because Salesforce will need the flow's ID later.A custom flow is one YAML file in the flow registry v1 syntax. This one has a single agent. When Salesforce starts the flow, it sends the error details as the flow's goal. The agent reads them as context:goal, investigates the repository, and opens one issue.version: "v1" environment: ambient components: - name: "sf_error_triage" type: AgentComponent prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt" inputs: - from: "context:project_id" as: "project_id" - from: "context:goal" as: "error_report" toolset: - "find_files" # locate the class or Flow in the repository - "grep" - "read_file" - "list_commits" # find recent changes to that file - "create_issue" # the only write: open the triage issue prompts: - prompt_id: "sf_error_triage_prompt" prompt_template: system: | You triage Salesforce runtime errors for a team that keeps its Salesforce metadata (Apex classes, triggers, Flows) in this project. You receive an error report with a class name, exception type, message and stack trace. 1. Find the source file for the class or Flow named in the report. 2. Read the code around the lines in the stack trace. 3. List recent commits that touched that file and identify any change that plausibly introduced the error. 4. Create one issue: - Title: " <exception type> in <class>" - Label: salesforce-error - Description: the original error, then sections for Likely cause, Affected component, Suspect change, Suggested next step, and Confidence (high, medium or low, with one line of reasoning). Rules: - Cite file paths, line numbers and commit SHAs for every claim. - If you cannot find the code or a suspect commit, say so. Do not guess. - Do not change code. A person decides what happens next. user: | Project ID: {{project_id}} Error report: {{error_report}} placeholder: history routers: - from: "sf_error_triage" to: "end" flow: entry_point: "sf_error_triage" The toolset is deliberately narrow: four tools read and one creates an issue. The flow can't push code or change existing issues, which makes it easy to review and easy to trust.Two lines in the prompt do the most work. Requiring a citation for every claim lets an engineer check the reasoning in a minute. Allowing "not found" stops the agent from inventing a cause.To create the flow, go to your project, select AI > Flows > New flow, choose Flow, paste the YAML, and select Create flow. You can also build and test it in VS Code with the GitLab flow builder.Step 2: Enable the flow and get its consumer IDA flow must be enabled in a project before anything can run it.In your project, select AI > Flows, open the Managed tab, and select your flow.Select Enable and choose the project that holds your Salesforce code. GitLab creates a service account for the flow, named ai-<flow>-<group>. The flow runs with a composite identity, so it can never access more than the user who starts it. When Salesforce starts the flow through the API, GitLab runs it as this service account.You don't need a mention or assign trigger. Salesforce will start this flow through the API.To start a custom flow through the API, Salesforce passes the flow's ai_catalog_item_consumer_id. Look it up with a short GraphQL query from the docs, and use the number at the end of the returned gid://gitlab/AiCatalogItemConsumer/<number>. Note it, along with the project ID.Finally, create a project access token with the api scope and at least the Developer role. Salesforce will use it to call GitLab. With a lower role, the API refuses to run catalog flows.Step 3: Call the flow from SalesforceStore the token in a Named Credential. Create a Named Credential called GitLab_API with the URL https://gitlab.com, backed by an External Credential that sends your project access token in the PRIVATE-TOKEN header. The token never appears in code.Call the Flows API from a Queueable. Salesforce doesn't allow callouts in the middle of saving a record, so the call runs as a background job. The job turns the exception into the flow's goal and starts the flow:public with sharing class DuoTriageJob implements Queueable, Database.AllowsCallouts { private final String goal; public DuoTriageJob(Exception e, String className) { goal = 'Class: ' + className + '
Exception: ' + e.getTypeName() + '
Message: ' + e.getMessage() + '
Stack trace:
' + e.getStackTraceString(); } public void execute(QueueableContext ctx) { Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt cfg = Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt.getInstance('Default'); HttpRequest req = new HttpRequest(); req.setEndpoint('callout:GitLab_API/api/v4/ai/duo_workflows/workflows'); req.setMethod('POST'); req.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json'); req.setBody(JSON.serialize(new Map<String, Object>{ 'project_id' => cfg.Project_Id__c, 'ai_catalog_item_consumer_id' => cfg.Consumer_Id__c.intValue(), 'goal' => goal, 'start_workflow' => true, 'allow_agent_to_request_user' => false, 'agent_privileges' => new List<Integer>{ 1, 2, 3 }, 'pre_approved_agent_privileges' => new List<Integer>{ 1, 2, 3 } })); HttpResponse res = new Http().send(req); // 201 Created: the response includes web_url, a link to the agent session. } } The project ID and consumer ID from Step 2 live in a custom metadata type, Duo_Triage_Setting__mdt, so you can change them without a deployment.Three settings in the request body do the most work:allow_agent_to_request_user: false means the flow runs to completion without pausing for questions. Nobody is watching a Salesforce error at 2 a.m.agent_privileges limits the agent to reading files (1), reading GitLab (2), and writing to GitLab (3), which it needs to create the issue. It can't run commands or use Git. List all privileges to check the IDs on your instance.pre_approved_agent_privileges repeats the same list, so the flow never stops to wait for tool approval.This example leaves out response checks, retries, and tests. Add them before you go to production.Step 4: Start the flow automatically or on demandAutomatically. Queue the job wherever your code catches and handles an exception:try { OpportunityDiscountService.applyTierDiscount(opportunities); } catch (Exception e) { System.enqueueJob(new DuoTriageJob(e, 'OpportunityDiscountService')); // ...your existing error handling } If the whole transaction is rolled back, Salesforce discards the queued job too, so place the call where your code handles the error and carries on.On demand. Some teams would rather choose which errors are worth investigating. Wrap the job in an invocable Apex action, label it Ask GitLab Duo to investigate, and add it to a screen flow that runs as a quick action on the record where you keep errors, such as a log record or a support case. One click in Salesforce, and the issue appears in GitLab a few minutes later.Step 5: What your team seesA user saves an Opportunity, an Apex trigger throws, and a few minutes later a new issue appears in the GitLab project. Here is an illustrative example of what the flow writes:##  System.NullPointerException in OpportunityDiscountService Label: salesforce-error ### Original error Attempt to de-reference a null object Class.OpportunityDiscountService.applyTierDiscount: line 48, column 1 Trigger.OpportunityTrigger: line 12, column 1 ### Likely cause applyTierDiscount() reads opp.Account.Tier__c without a null check (line 48). Opportunities saved without an Account reach this line with opp.Account == null. ### Affected component force-app/main/default/classes/OpportunityDiscountService.cls, called from OpportunityTrigger (before update). ### Suspect change Commit 3f9c2ab, "Apply tier discount on stage change", added the Tier__c lookup. Before that commit, the method returned early when AccountId was blank. ### Suggested next step Restore the early return for a blank AccountId, or guard the lookup. Add a test that updates an Opportunity with no Account. ### Confidence High. The stack trace line matches the new code in 3f9c2ab. Nothing in Salesforce or the codebase changed. The flow did the first round of investigation and left the decision to an engineer: fix it now, schedule it, or close it as expected behavior.The Flows API response includes a web_url for the agent session. Open it to see each step the flow took, which is the fastest way to tune the prompt.Guardrails for productionBefore you run this in production, check these points. They decide whether the pattern holds up under real traffic.Send the shape of the error, not the data. Strip record IDs, emails, and free text that may hold customer data from the message before it leaves Salesforce. Review what the goal contains with your security team before you turn this on.Grant the fewest privileges. Reading files, reading GitLab, and creating an issue are enough. Expand the flow, for example to open merge requests, only after it has earned trust with accurate analysis.Scope the token. Use a project access token for one project, not a personal token, and rotate it on a schedule.Keep a person in charge. The flow investigates; an engineer decides. Citations in every issue let the engineer verify the reasoning instead of redoing it.One platform, from error to fixFollow that error from start to finish:GitLab Duo investigates it. The flow reads the stack trace, finds the code, and points to the change that most likely caused the error.A GitLab issue tracks it. The analysis becomes work the team can label, prioritize, assign, and plan into a milestone, like any other issue.GitLab CI/CD runs it and ships the fix. The flow itself runs on GitLab CI/CD, and so does your Salesforce deployment pipeline. An engineer opens a merge request from the issue, the pipeline validates and deploys the change to Salesforce, and the issue closes when the merge request merges.Because every step happens in GitLab, the trail stays connected. The issue links to the merge request, the merge request to its pipeline, and the pipeline to the deployment. Anyone can see what broke, why, who fixed it, and when the fix reached production.Beyond Salesforce errorsStrip away the Salesforce details and the pattern is simple: a business system makes one HTTP call, and a custom GitLab Duo flow that knows your code does the investigation. title: [Engineering at Meta] Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
summary: Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production. Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests. Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale. Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch. In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives. The Advantage of Catching JiTTests Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not. Table 1. Key differences between traditional LLM-based code review and Catching JiTTests. How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives). It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers? To address this, we developed two tandem workflows: An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points. A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”). Figure 1. The architecture of the dodgy diff and intent-aware workflows for Catching JiTTests. To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives. We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch. How It Works The entire system workflow happens in five stages: Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions. Stage 2: Two Diff-Aware Test-Generation Workflows The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them. At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks”— the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent. Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent). Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches. Stage 3: LLM-as-Judge Ensemble (Automated Assessment) Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive). The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review: The weak-catch test-case code. The test-execution outcome (failure code, message, execution trace). The code changes between parent and child (the diff). The inferred diff intent. Stage 4: Rule-Based Assessor (RubFake) We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake). LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration. Stage 5: Human-on-the-Loop (Engineer Reach-Out) Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers. Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human-on-the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output. Table 2. Operational differences between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop approaches. The Impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results. As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives. In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe. Figure 2. The impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta in the first half of 2026. Why It Matters Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended. The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item. Read the Paper Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale, details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure.
